change.title: pr-33832-flat
change.description: Add AuthzClientCryptoProvider for authorization client cryptographic operations
change.author: Cristian Sotomayor

findings.title: Two providers with the same order are now picked silently, which can mean a non-FIPS provider in a FIPS setup
findings.body: Before this change, finding more than one CryptoProvider threw an IllegalStateException. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first one is used. The only trace of the others is a debug log (lines 64-70). DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so when two of them are on the classpath together the stable sort leaves them in ServiceLoader (classpath) order. That is the same misconfiguration that used to fail at startup. In a FIPS deployment that accidentally ships crypto-default, the server can now start on the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider without any visible warning. This affects every caller that relies on detection: `KeycloakApplication` (services/.../KeycloakApplication.java:89) and admin-cli `Globals` (Globals.java:44). Quarkus is not affected because it calls `setProvider` explicitly. Suggested fix: still throw when the two highest-ranked providers have the same `order()`, so only the authz-client fallback (100) can lose quietly. Logging the ignored providers at warn level would also help.

findings.title: Dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 build two `ASN1Encoder` instances and throw them away. Lines 119-120 build the same values again. You can delete the two lines.

findings.title: Test only round-trips through the new code and never checks the DER against the JDK
findings.body: The test decodes the JDK signature, re-encodes it with the new `ASN1Encoder` and decodes it again with the new `ASN1Decoder`. If the encoder and decoder share the same mistake, the test still passes. Call `Signature.initVerify(publicKey)` and `verify(asn1Des)` (or compare `asn1Des` with `sign`), which checks the produced DER against the JDK. Also, one default `KeyPairGenerator("EC")` key (P-256 or P-384, depending on the JDK) is used for all three algorithms. So ES512 never runs with a P-521 key, where r and s are 66 bytes and can carry a leading sign byte, which is the case the padding and truncation in `integerToBytes` exist for. Generating a key on the matching curve for each algorithm would cover it.

contracts.action: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) calls CryptoIntegration.init with the authz-client classloader
contracts.equivalent_path: KeycloakApplication / admin-cli Globals call CryptoIntegration.init(cl) the same way
contracts.before_after: init is guarded by a double-checked lock and keeps the first detected provider for the whole JVM; BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER (static final) then reads getBouncyCastleProvider(), which for AuthzClientCryptoProvider is the default KeyStore provider
contracts.visible_effect: ECDSAAlgorithm static helpers work in the authz client without BouncyCastle
contracts.failure_mode: If no provider is found, init throws IllegalStateException out of create(). If the authz client initializes first in a JVM that also needs full crypto, the limited provider stays cached for the whole JVM and other operations throw UnsupportedOperationException

summary: This change adds a lightweight CryptoProvider for the authz client and replaces the old "multiple providers" error with selection by `order()`. Main concern: Default, Elytron and FIPS all return order 200. A classpath that holds two of them used to fail at startup; now one is picked silently, which can mean a non-FIPS provider in a FIPS setup on paths that rely on detection. Smaller points: two dead encoder lines, and a test that only round-trips through the new code and never checks the DER against the JDK or covers a P-521 key.
